name: 11-moondeck
description: The developer console: one page that builds, flashes, tests and checks the project, and why it is ours rather than PlatformIO.

steps.title: MoonDeck
steps.caption: MoonDeck. One console, every target.

This is MoonDeck, the console the project is developed from. It runs in a browser on your own machine, and every button on it is a script in the repository. One command starts it: uv run moondeck slash moondeck dot py.

The obvious question first: why not PlatformIO. The ESP32 build here is native to Espressif's own framework, tracking pre-release versions against a pinned commit for chips like the P4, which a packaged platform does not let you do.
And the drivers reach for the vendor's own peripherals directly, rather than through an Arduino layer that would sit between the code and the hardware it is timing.
But the real reason is the size of the job. Compile, upload and monitor is three of these buttons. The rest is everything else a day's work needs.
Desktop is the first tab, and the one used most. MoonLight runs on this computer as a real device, so almost everything is proven here before any hardware is touched.
Build compiles the firmware for this machine, in seconds rather than the minutes a chip build takes.
Run starts it, and the interface you have seen in the other clips is then live on this computer, with no device plugged in anywhere.
Test is the group that keeps the agents honest. Two thousand unit tests, the scenario suite that drives a whole pipeline, and the host tests for the scripts themselves.
Check is the group that reads the repository rather than running it: specs against code, documentation against what generates it, the platform boundary, the catalogs.
Repo health is the one worth knowing about. It measures flash, memory and speed every commit, so a regression shows up as a number rather than as a feeling months later.
Tools is the deeper analysis: static analysis, the hot path, complexity. Slower, so they are run when something is being changed rather than on every commit.
And docs builds the documentation site and the screenshots in it, from the same repository, so the published pages cannot drift from the code.
The second tab is the chip itself. Setup fetches the framework, build compiles the firmware, flash writes it over USB, and monitor shows the serial output.
That is the compile, upload and monitor a normal tool gives you, and it is one group of one tab here. Erase sits beside it, and asks before it runs.
There is also an emulator, which runs the firmware with no chip attached at all: useful for the boot path when the device is not on the desk.
The third tab is live, and it drives real devices over the network rather than building anything.
Live scenarios are the same tests the scenario clip ran, run against hardware on your bench instead of against this computer.
And video records these clips. The one you are watching was made by a button on this page, driving the interface the way a person would.
Forty six of them, across three tabs. Every one is a script that runs the same way from a terminal, so a person, an agent and the build server all take the identical path.
